query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Brief History of Blue

Blue is everywhere now: jeans, police uniforms, corporate logos, hospital signs, social media icons, the sky in children’s drawings. But for much of human history, blue was strangely elusive.

Ancient peoples saw the sky and the sea, of course, but blue was difficult to capture, name, and make permanent. Unlike red from ochre, black from charcoal, or yellow from earth pigments, strong blue pigments were rare. In many early languages, words for blue appeared later than words for black, white, red, and yellow. The colour existed in nature, but it was not always culturally prominent.

One of the earliest great blues came from **ancient Egypt**. Around the third millennium BCE, Egyptians developed **Egyptian blue**, often considered the first synthetic pigment. It was made by heating sand, copper minerals, and lime. The result was a vivid blue used on tomb paintings, statues, jewellery, and decorative objects. For Egyptians, blue was associated with the Nile, the heavens, fertility, rebirth, and divine protection. The hair and beards of gods were sometimes shown in blue, linking them to the celestial and eternal.

Elsewhere, blue remained rare and expensive. In the ancient Mediterranean world, purple often carried more prestige than blue. The Greeks and Romans used blue, but it did not yet have the noble status it would later acquire. Romans sometimes associated blue clothing with foreigners or lower-status groups. To them, a bright blue-dyed garment could seem strange, even barbaric.

The great transformation of blue came in the **Middle Ages**.

In Christian Europe, blue gradually became the colour of the Virgin Mary. Earlier images of Mary often showed her in dark or varied colours, but from the twelfth century onward, artists increasingly dressed her in brilliant blue robes. This was partly theological and partly material. The most precious blue pigment was **ultramarine**, made from lapis lazuli mined mainly in Afghanistan and transported across vast trade routes. Its name means “from beyond the sea.” Ultramarine was more expensive than gold, so using it for Mary signalled reverence, purity, and sacred importance.

As Mary’s blue grew in religious art, the colour’s reputation changed. Blue became associated with humility, truth, loyalty, and heaven. Kings and nobles began adopting it. The French monarchy made blue a royal colour, especially through the deep blue field scattered with golden fleurs-de-lis. By the late medieval period, blue had climbed from relative obscurity to one of Europe’s most prestigious colours.

Blue also entered daily life through dye. The main European source was **woad**, a plant that produced a blue dye after a lengthy and rather unpleasant fermentation process. Later, **indigo**, grown in Asia, Africa, and the Americas, became a major global commodity. Indigo was stronger and cheaper than woad, and its trade reshaped economies. But this history also has a brutal side: in the colonial era, indigo plantations relied heavily on exploited and enslaved labour. The beautiful dye carried with it histories of empire, coercion, and resistance.

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, blue became increasingly democratic. New chemical pigments changed everything. **Prussian blue**, discovered accidentally in Berlin in the early 1700s, was one of the first modern synthetic pigments. It was cheaper than ultramarine and quickly spread through painting, printing, textiles, and decoration. Later came synthetic ultramarine and other industrial blues, making the colour widely accessible.

Artists loved blue’s emotional range. It could be celestial, melancholy, cold, infinite, spiritual, or modern. In Japanese woodblock prints, imported Prussian blue helped create intense landscapes and seascapes, including Hokusai’s famous wave. In Europe, Romantic painters used blue for distance and longing. Picasso’s **Blue Period** turned the colour into a language of poverty, grief, and solitude. In the twentieth century, Yves Klein created his own intense matte blue, **International Klein Blue**, treating the colour almost as an immaterial force.

Blue also became political and social. It appeared in military uniforms, national flags, workwear, and institutions. Navy blue suggested discipline and authority. Pale blue could suggest innocence or cleanliness. Dark blue became a colour of business suits, banks, and reliability. In the United States and many other places, blue jeans transformed indigo-dyed work clothing into a global symbol of youth, labour, rebellion, and casual style.

Today, blue is often described as the world’s favourite colour. It dominates technology branding because it seems trustworthy, calm, rational, and safe. Banks, airlines, medical companies, and social platforms use it to project stability. Yet blue still carries older meanings too: sadness in “the blues,” divinity in sacred art, depth in the ocean, distance in the horizon, and freedom in the open sky.

The history of blue is therefore a history of rarity becoming familiarity. Once hard to make, it became holy. Once costly, it became royal. Once royal, it became industrial. Once industrial, it became ordinary. And yet it has never become dull. Blue remains the colour of what is near and unreachable at the same time: the cloth on our bodies, the screen in our hands, the sky above us, and the far edge of the world.
